power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Factors Associated with Meaning in Life Among Hispanic Adults in the Post-Pandemic Period: A Cross-Sectional Study Across 16 Countries

text.text: This cross-sectional study examined post-pandemic levels of meaning in life and its associated factors among Hispanic adults (N = 10,142) aged 18 to 78 years old, residing across 16 countries.
Analysis revealed that 50.2% of the participants experienced low levels of meaning in life.

Controlling for fixed country effects, mental health, occupational purpose, gratitude, friendships, and engagement in meaningful activities emerged as variables associated with higher meaning in life.
Conversely, low perceived workplace success, absence of gratitude, and heavy social media consumption were linked to lower meaning.
Key sociodemographic markers, including income, education, and gender, showed no significant associations with meaning in life.
This non-significance suggests that meaning in life functions as an accessible resource available to individuals regardless of their sociodemographic factors.

These findings indicate that post-pandemic recovery across Hispanic populations must extend beyond economic indicators to prioritize accessible community-based mental health integration and social infrastructure, offering an evidencebased starting point for designing culturally grounded interventions to promote meaning in life.

The COVID-19 pandemic represented an unprecedented disruption to global public health, imposing severe psychological distress by exacerbating mental health challenges, and destabilizing social structures by fracturing daily routines, relational networks, and occupational stability.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO) (2022) there was a 25% increase in prevalence of anxiety and depression worldwide after lockdown.
Specifically, in Latin America, studies show that around 20% to 70% of the population continues to suffer from depression and anxiety after the pandemic (Pan American Health Organization, 2021).
In this post-pandemic context, restoring psychological well-being has emerged as a central priority for behavioral health.

Among psychological resources, meaning in life, understood as the affective and cognitive perception of values that guide individuals to act in a particular way, fostering coherence and personal identity (Martínez, 2007), functions as a vital buffer against psychological challenges (Dulaney et al., 2018).

text.text: From Viktor Frankl's logotherapy to contemporary models of well-being, meaning in life has been consistently included as a central component of psychological health (Disabato et al., 2025; Ryff, 1989; Seligman, 2011).

text.text: However, the relative importance of these factors, and how they operate in Hispanic communities remains largely understudied.

Particularly in Latin America, empirical research aimed at better understanding the specific affective experiences and motivational cues associated with meaning in life remains scarce, as research has predominantly focused on psychometric studies to validate different instruments, leaving its associated variables comparatively understudied (Caycho-Rodríguez et al., 2023; Simkin et al., 2018; Steger & Samman, 2012).

text.text: To address this limitation, we aim to provide the first large-sample descriptive account of meaning in life and its associated factors in a Hispanic sample.

Findings are intended to provide an evidence base for culturally grounded programs aimed at promoting meaning in life among Hispanic communities, which remain markedly underrepresented in the well-being literature relative to its global size.

The present study offers the potential to generate an empirical foundation for targeted behavioral health strategies, and key insights intended to inform future interventions for restoring psychological well-being in the postpandemic context.

This study employs a non-experimental cross-sectional design, since no intentional modifications of the variables were conducted to assess their effect on another; rather, the phenomena are observed as they occur in their natural context at a specific point in time (Mousalli-Kayat, 2015).

text.text: The sample was selected using a non-probabilistic convenience sampling method as participants were recruited via dissemination on social media.

The final sample comprised N = 10,142 individuals from 16 countries to ensure greater demographic diversity: Argentina (n = 366), Chile (n = 167), Colombia (n = 5,959), Costa Rica (n = 98), Ecuador (n = 163), El Salvador (n = 37), Spain (n = 124), United States (n = 89), Guatemala (n = 133), Honduras (n = 41), Mexico (n = 2,211), Panama (n = 30), Peru (n = 101), Dominican Republic (n = 60), Uruguay (n = 43), and Venezuela (n = 520).
Participants range in age from 18 to 78 years (M =42.3, SD =9.9).
Approximately 85.9% were women.

text.text: As inclusion criteria participants were required to be over 18 years of age and be Hispanic.
It is important to emphasize that all participants took part in the study voluntarily and were informed of its research purpose through the informed consent process.
Instruments (EDSV) (Martínez et al., 2011).

text.text: This scale assesses meaning in life, understood as the affective-cognitive perception of referential values that drive a person and prompt them to act in a particular way, providing personal identity and coherence with oneself.
It comprises 18 items rated on a four-point Likert scale; the final score is obtained by calculating the average score.

Lower scores reflect a lower perceived meaning in life, labelled as "Search for meaning," whereas higher scores indicate a stronger level of meaning, labelled and interpreted as "Meaning fulfillment levels".
Psychometric evaluation shows that the scale has optimal internal consistency (α = 0.94).
An ad hoc questionnaire, specifically designed for this study in Spanish, was administered.

It comprised 19 questions addressing various aspects of daily life, including friendships, hobbies, gratitude, engagement with material possessions, romantic relationships, religious practices, health perception, social media use, purpose in the occupation, and perceived work success, alongside sociodemographic variables (Dulaney et al., 2018; Grouden & Jose, 2015; Hadden & Knee, 2016; Hooker et al., 2019; Silver et al., 2021).

This approach is consistent with previous research showing that single-item measures can provide useful and valid assessments when the variable represents a global evaluation, a concrete behavior, or a straightforward aspect of respondents' lives (Bowling, 2005; Elo et al., 2003; Spörrle & Bekk, 2014).

text.text: The ad hoc questionnaire and the EDSV were uploaded to a platform that enabled large-scale distribution.
Participants were recruited through dissemination on social media through non-paid advertisements posted on Instagram between August and October 2024.
Subsequently, the dataset was downloaded, and an initial analysis was conducted to remove inconsistent responses as part of a quality control procedure.

Responses were screened for eligibility and completeness, a total of 10,280 individuals accessed the survey, after excluding participants who did not meet the inclusion criteria and those with incomplete responses, the final sample consisted of 10,142 participants.
All statistical analyses were performed in R using the RStudio environment.

In accordance with the guidelines established by the Ministry of Health and Social Protection (1993), which sets forth the scientific, technical, and administrative standards for health research, this study adhered to criteria related to informed consent, confidentiality of information, and protection of participants' privacy, with prior authorization obtained from all individuals.

Both the study protocol and the informed consent form were developed according to the Declaration of Helsinki (2013) and were submitted to and approved by the Institution's Ethics Committee in session 02 which took place in July 2024.
The study was classified as a no-risk investigation given its evaluative nature, as no interventions were performed on the participants.

To assess the suitability of a multilevel model in the analysis of meaning in life, the proportion of variability explained by the group level (country) was examined using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).
The ICC was calculated from a null model in which the dependent variable (meaning in life) was modeled with a random intercept at the country level.
The result obtained was ICC = 0.0011, indicating that approximately 0.11% of the variance in meaning in life is due to differences between countries.
Given that ICC values above 0.05 (5%) typically justify the need for a multilevel model (Hox et al., 2017), the result suggests that variability in meaning in life across countries is minimal.
text.formatted: Given that ICC values above 0.05 (5%) typically justify the need for a multilevel model <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hox et al., 2017)</ref>, the result suggests that variability in meaning in life across countries is minimal.

text.text: This indicates that the country does not introduce substantial variability in the dependent variable, thus limiting the usefulness of a random-effects model.

Therefore, a linear regression model with fixed country effects was estimated, using ordinary least squares to control for systematic differences between countries without assuming an unnecessary multilevel structure.
Regarding the variable of interest, the original distribution of meaning in life exhibited a tendency toward negative skewness.
To address this issue, a logarithmic transformation was applied to reduce skewness and improve the approximation to normality.
The transformation produced a more symmetric distribution, closer to normality, thereby enhancing variance stability and facilitating the interpretation of model coefficients.
This suggests that the model estimated with the transformed variable provides greater statistical robustness and stability.

text.text: A greater number of friends is associated with increased meaning in life, highlighting the role of social relationships in fostering meaning.
Children also emerged as a relevant variable, with individuals reporting a higher number of children experiencing greater meaning.
In contrast, extensive use of social media appears to have negative effects, which become noticeable when usage exceeds three hours per day.
However, moderate social media use: one hour per day (p = .333) or between two or three (p = .957) did not have a clear association with meaning.
Perceived romantic involvement also shows nuanced associations: individuals who are not in love, or who feel very slightly in love, report lower levels of perceived meaning in life.
Individuals who reported doing a higher number of meaningful activities exhibited higher meaning in life, as did those who perceived their occupation to be highly meaningful.
Conversely, individuals reporting low levels of purpose in their occupation and low levels of perceived success at the workplace presented lower levels of meaning in life.
This highlights the role of occupational factors in fostering meaning.
Individuals reporting a more positive perception of their mental health exhibited higher meaning in life.

Frequent and consistent use of material possessions is positively associated with a greater sense of meaning in life, indicating that the capacity to enjoy personal resources may shape perceptions of subjective well-being.
In a similar vein, belief in God and perceptions of better physical health appear to exert a modest positive effect.

However, the belief in God with doubts (p = .563) did not show a clear association with meaning, as well as the levels of religious commitment, both low (p = .440) and high levels of engagement (p =.616) showed no clear association with meaning.
Sociodemographic variables did not exhibit statistically significant effects in the model, which suggests that their relationship with meaning in life is inconclusive within this sample.
These variables include gender (p = .101), level of education (p = .302), income (p = .289), and occupation: employee (p = .118), student (p = .822), or independent worker (p =.147).

This study provides, to our knowledge, the largest descriptive account to date of meaning in life and its associated variables among Hispanic communities, drawing on a sample of 10,142 participants across 16 countries in the post-pandemic period.
The primary objective of this study was to characterize the state of meaning in life and identify its associated factors in the post-pandemic era.

Our findings indicate that half of the sample (50.2%) reported low levels of meaning in life, underscoring that diminished meaning is not a marginal experience within this sample but affects a substantial portion of respondents.
This finding is noteworthy as, according to Heintzelman and King (2014), meaning in life is apparently typical and the average life is very meaningful.

text.text: The disruption of long-term life plans, economic shifts, and altered social dynamics appear to coincide with an active state of searching for purpose among an important proportion of Hispanic adults within this sample.

Regarding specific associated factors, variables reflecting social support, occupational purpose, and attitudinal choices emerged as primary elements tied to meaning, being consistent with Viktor Frankl's (1967 , 1991) theories regarding the possible pathways to discovering meaning.

text.text: Concerning relational support, our results indicate that friends, children, and romantic involvement were associated with meaning.
This pattern of findings could be understood in the light of collectivistic cultures, as Hispanic communities tend to gravitate toward more collectivist tendencies.

In these cultures, the sources of meaning may differ from individualistic societies as they place less emphasis on the personal self, which could include personality and strengths, and more on the collective self, which could include social roles (Ortiz, 2020).

text.text: Therefore, the experience of meaning in Hispanic samples could be rooted in a collectivist culture that values relationships.

In contrast, heavy social media consumption was associated with lower meaning, suggesting that the hours spent in these platforms may disrupt authentic social connection and well-being, possibly through passive social comparison (Valerio & Serna, 2018; World Happiness Report, 2026).

text.text: In relation to occupational factors, our findings emphasize that a lack of perceived purpose in one's occupation is linked to lower levels of meaning in life, whereas perceiving a significantly elevated level of purpose is related to higher levels of meaning.

This outcome aligns with the evidence reported by Eakman and Eklund (2012), who identified occupational purpose and occupational value as the primary variables of life satisfaction and meaning in life in regression models, suggesting that participation in work, study, caregiving, and other meaningful activities is a fundamental aspect of human life.

text.text: Similarly, low levels of perceived success at the workplace were associated with meaning, which shows the importance of the self-evaluation of one's performance at work for well-being.

This could be interpreted in the light of self-efficacy, as individuals who perceive themselves as less successful may also experience weaker beliefs in their ability to achieve valued goals and effectively influence major events.
Lower self-efficacy, in turn, may be associated with a diminished sense of meaning and purpose (Cavazos Vela et al., 2018).

text.text: Notably, income, educational attainment, employment status, and gender did not show an association with meaning in life.

This finding holds substantial social and clinical importance: it demonstrates that meaning in life functions as an accessible resource, regardless of the sociodemographic characteristics of each individual.
This is consistent with Frankl's (1991) theory of meaning as a fundamental human motivation, as the capacity to search for and discover meaning is inherent to human existence.

text.text: A key finding of this study is that country-level variation accounted for a minimal proportion of the overall variance in meaning in life.
This suggests that rather than being dictated by macro-level national differences, meaning in life is rooted in shared individual and relational processes.

This interpretation is consistent with cross-national research in Latin America showing substantial comparability in the underlying construct of purpose in life across countries (Caycho-Rodríguez et al., 2023).

text.text: While Hispanic populations may differ in their sociocultural and national contexts, the experience of meaning may be relatively consistent within this sample, which has implications for the development of regional public policies and behavioral health interventions.

Consequently, these findings offer a starting point for designing interventions to promote meaning in life among Hispanic samples that are centered in relational and culturally salient pathways, rather than defaulting to intervention models developed primarily in individualist cultural contexts.

Programs that strengthen relational support networks, foster a sense of purpose within occupational and social roles, and cultivate gratitude may be particularly well-aligned with how meaning is constructed within these cultural frameworks, though this remains to be assessed directly through intervention research.
Thus, clinical and community programs should incorporate these strategies in their interventions in order to promote meaning in life.

Similarly, organizations employing Hispanic workforces should prioritize employee agency, task significance, and alignment between organizational goals and individual values to avoid quiet quitting and foster meaning (Magrizos et al., 2026).

text.text: Future research should prioritize probabilistic sampling designs to establish representative estimates, incorporate longitudinal designs capable of testing directional and reciprocal relationships between these variables, and examine whether collectivism operates as an explicit mediator of the associations identified here, rather than as an inferred contextual explanation.
This study has some limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results.

First, the recruitment procedure may have introduced selection bias, as participants with a greater pre-existing interest in meaning in life may have been more likely to volunteer for the study, similarly, individuals without internet access, with lower social media engagement, or from groups less likely to encounter recruitment materials could be underrepresented.
This also resulted in a sample predominantly female and concentrated in Colombia and Mexico, limiting population-wide generalizability.
Second, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inferences; therefore, the identified relationships reflect concurrent associations.

Third, references to post-pandemic increases in mental health difficulties draw on prior longitudinal literature rather than on data collected in the present study, which captured a single time point.
Future studies should employ longitudinal designs to observe the dynamic relationships between mental health, occupational purpose, social relationships, and meaning over time.
This study provides broad empirical evidence regarding the factors associated with meaning in life among Hispanic adults in the post-pandemic period.

By analyzing data from 10,142 individuals across 16 nations, our results demonstrate that meaning in life is strongly tied to mental health, occupational purpose, gratitude, and social support networks.
In the wake of the global disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, understanding these mechanisms has become an essential priority for Hispanic behavioral health.

These findings offer practical insights for behavioral health professionals, researchers, and policy-makers seeking to design interventions that enhance meaning in life throughout Hispanic populations.

However, those interventions should move beyond broad economic metrics, and instead, prioritize culturally tailored, community-based strategies that foster social connectedness, workplace agency, and cultivate psychological resources like gratitude.
Strengthening these actionable domains offers a promising, accessible pathway to promote psychological wellbeing and meaning in life across Hispanic communities.
